text:
maria: Seeing a spike in GPU pod pending again — latency on the image-generation queue jumped at 08:07 UTC.
maria: `kubectl get pods -o wide | grep Pending | grep gpu` shows a bunch of `CrashLoopBackOff` / `Pending` with `0/1 nodes are available: Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu.`

raj: Thanks, pinging infra. Do we have available GPU nodepool capacity in us-west1? IIRC autoscaler max for gpu-pool is 20 nodes.

elliot: autoscaler logs look funny — CA didn't scale up even though pods were unschedulable. I saw this earlier when HPA was spinning up replicas quickly.

karen: Can you paste the pod events? Might be taint/toleration mismatch or the pods are requesting fractional GPUs (we saw bugs there).

maria: paste events:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  2m    default-scheduler  0/20 nodes are available: 20 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu.
```

maria: CA logs snippet:
```
I0308 08:07:05 autoscaler.go:512] No unschedulable pods
I0308 08:07:05 scale_up.go:137] No scale-up: found 0 candidates
```

raj: Hmm `No unschedulable pods` usually means the pods aren't marked as unschedulable because the scheduler isn't marking them correctly — or they were filtered out by a predicate (nodeSelector/taint).

elliot: Another possibility: HPA increased replicas quickly but pods are Pending with `PodFitsResources` failing. If the pods have `nodeSelector: gpu=true` and there are 0 nodes of that label, CA will scale node pool only if pod is unschedulable and matches nodegroup provisioning rules.

karen: Also check if the pods have `tolerations` that match the GPU node taint. We added `NoSchedule` taint to preemptible-gpu nodes last month to protect stable workloads.

maria: Confirmed pods have `nodeSelector: accelerator: nvidia-tesla-a100` and toleration for `gpu-warm:NoSchedule` is missing. But CA still should detect unschedulable when resources insufficient.

raj: Do we use Prometheus adapter custom metrics for HPA? If HPA scales based on `queue_latency` instead of actual pod Ready state, it can cause a rapid surge of replicas that are still Pending waiting for GPUs. CA should react though.

elliot: There is a known race: HPA triggers new replicas -> scheduler tries -> pod is Pending because of GPU resource -> but if pods specify strict `nodeAffinity` that matches an autoscaled nodegroup name (e.g., `cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool: gpu-pool-1`), CA won't scale new nodepool because it won't know how to provision nodes that satisfy that affinity unless nodepool exists.

karen: We had that exact misconfiguration. Some deployments pin to nodepool names. CA can't create a nodepool that matches an affinity to a non-existent nodepool label.

maria: Our Deployment spec uses `nodeSelector: nodepool: gpu-pool` (bad) since we thought it would ensure GPU placement. That's likely preventing CA.

raj: Actionable steps:
- Remove hard `nodeSelector: nodepool` and instead use `nodeSelector: accelerator: nvidia` + tolerations for `gpu:NoSchedule`.
- Ensure CA has access to the GPU node pool (minSize < maxSize, quotas ok) and expander strategy is `least-waste`.
- Add a small buffer: keep 1-2 warm GPU nodes with taint `gpu-warm=true:NoSchedule` and `podToleration` for critical pods, so critical burst can land immediately.

elliot: Also check the Prometheus adapter mapping: if HPA uses `queue_latency` from `keda` or `prom-adapter`, a misconfigured adapter can return NaN causing HPA to mis-evaluate. Run:
```
kubectl get --raw "/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/pods/queue_latency" | jq .
```

karen: VPA note: we had VPA enabled cluster-wide and it tried to recommend more CPU for the sidecar, which pushed requests up and made pods request more GPU memory implicitly via fused resources — for GPU workloads VPA is usually a bad idea. Check for `VerticalPodAutoscaler` targeting this deployment.

maria: I see a VPA for `image-gen` in default namespace. I will evict VPA for this deployment.

infra-oncall: Also be aware of regional quota: us-west1 has GPU quota 40, and two other teams are using 30 currently. If CA tries to add more nodes beyond region quota it will fail silently. Check cloud quota dashboard.

raj: Good call — if quota is hit, CA will log `quota exceeded` in cloud provider events. Look at cloud-controller-manager events.

autoscaler-bot: [auto-alert] 08:09 UTC: GPU nodepool `gpu-pool-1` reached max size 20. Pending pods: 12.

maria: Okay, plan I'm going to execute now (will update here):
1) remove `nodepool` nodeSelector from Deployment and switch to `accelerator` label + add tolerations
2) disable VPA for this deployment
3) create 2 warm nodes in `gpu-pool-1` with taint `gpu-warm=true:NoSchedule` and allow critical pods via toleration
4) verify CA expander set to `least-waste` and `--scale-down-unneeded-time=10m`

raj: Sounds good. After that, if CA still doesn't scale, we can create a minimal `ClusterAutoscaler` fallback policy to allow emergency scale to other nodepools or spin up spot GPUs in another region temporarily.

elliot: Long-term: we should stop using hard nodepool labels in manifests. Use `nodeAffinity` by hardware label (accelerator vendor/model) instead. And add a small GPU buffer (default 1 node) for all clusters that host GPU services.

karen: Also add a test in chaos-harness that simulates HPA surge while GPU nodes are zero to catch this in CI.

maria: Updating now. I'll post results in ~10m.

(10m later)

maria: Updates: removed bad nodeSelector and VPA. CA scaled up to 3 more nodes and 6 pods moved to Running. Latency dropped back to normal.

raj: Nice. Can you file a short postmortem and a change to our k8s deployment lint rules to block `nodeSelector: nodepool` in manifests? :memo:

maria: Will do. Thanks everyone. :pray:
